chapter_theme: Under the heading வீட்டு நெறி, thirteen verses on the way to release: self-mastery outranks wealth and birth, the senses must be guarded early, the finished household should give way to renunciation and the undecided lose both lives, no fortune escapes Death, desire and pride in town life are costly, the renouncer must cut even the smallest tie, and birth ends when its supports are gone.

387.reading: Wealth that does not run short however it is counted, good birth and the possessions that kings hold are set aside, and so is being named by kings as men of worth: for this life and the next, the verse says, owning oneself comes first.
387.nuance: தம்மை உடைமை, 'having oneself', is read here as self-mastery, the possession that the external goods of wealth, lineage and royal favour cannot replace; the verse ranks it above even a king's acknowledgement, the honour a court poet might value most.

pazhamozhi.literal: possessing oneself is the chief thing

story.act: no story; the proverb is set against a list of outer goods: uncounted wealth, birth, royal property and royal recognition

pazhamozhi.applied_to: self-mastery outranks wealth, birth and royal esteem in this world and the next

388.reading: Those who do not, early in life, guard the five so that they are held in check, grow excellent here by the three they have taken up, and so make a safeguard for the road taken when the body falls away, are said by the proverb to have set the drum upon the kolli.
388.nuance: The five are most naturally the senses; the three begun may be thought, word and deed, or in a Jain frame right faith, knowledge and conduct; the verse does not say. கொல்லி is obscure: if it stands for கொள்ளி, the funeral firebrand, the proverb mocks those who beat the drum only when the pyre is lit, which fits the verse's stress on சிறுகாலை, but this is a guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: they set the drum on the kolli

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who leave provision for the afterlife until too late

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the safeguard for the next world must be made early, by restraint of the senses

389.reading: Once a man has made friends, quieted his enmities, gone after and joined the sharp-toothed women with waists like the drum, and set up a household, the proverb asks what use after that is a body that does not renounce.
389.nuance: The household is not condemned: friendship, peace and marriage are listed as tasks completed, and the question falls only on what comes after them. Renunciation is cast as the use of the body, so the body that stays in the house past its work is called useless.
389.domain_note: a man whose household tasks are done

pazhamozhi.literal: what is the use of a body that does not renounce?

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the householder who has done everything the house asks

pazhamozhi.applied_to: after the household is complete, renunciation is the body's remaining use

390.reading: Those who take up neither the householder's life nor the life without a house, and stand in the middle while the good life passes, never resolving to go wholly to one side, are said by the proverb to have lost both ends of the carrying pole.
390.nuance: The verse does not rank the two lives; it condemns only the failure to choose. இருதலையும் கா கழித்தார் pictures the carrier's pole with a load at each end: the undecided drop both, so the image makes indecision itself a loss, not a neutral pause.

pazhamozhi.literal: they have lost both ends of the carrying pole

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who hover between household and renunciation

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one must commit wholly to one of the two lives, or lose both

391.reading: Wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and good birth may all be present, yet because Death is not turned aside by honouring or fearing it, the proverb asks who knows of anyone who leapt over Death and survived.
391.nuance: The construal of மதித்தஞ்சி மாறும் அஃதின்மையால் is not secure: it may mean that Death cannot be made to turn back by esteem or fear, or that the six goods give no way of escape for all that people value them. Either way the six goods are listed only to be cancelled at one stroke.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one knows of having leapt over Death and lived

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who trust in wealth, youth, beauty, strength and birth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no gift of fortune or birth exempts one from Death

392.reading: The hunger that besets the body, of no help to the three aims one keeps, is as old and as fertile as anything that has come down from of old; since what is eaten is known to go into the belly and turn foul, the proverb says one's own desire becomes an arrow, enters within and destroys.
392.nuance: The three that one keeps (கொண்டொழுகும் மூன்று) are probably aram, porul and inbam, which hunger serves none of. திச்சென்று is obscure and the reading 'turns foul' is a guess from context. அம்பாயுள் is divided here as அம்பு ஆய் உள், desire turning into an arrow against oneself; other divisions are possible.

pazhamozhi.literal: one's own desire becomes an arrow, enters within, and finishes one

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the craving of the belly for food that only turns to waste

pazhamozhi.applied_to: desire for food harms the one who feeds it

393.reading: Those who do not clearly weigh how far their wealth and their span of life will go with them, who swell with pride at a little and live delighting in the town instead of living in the hermitage, are said by the proverb to be eating the honey of the thorn bush.
393.nuance: பள்ளி is the dwelling of renouncers, in a Jain text likely the monks' retreat, set against பதி, the town. The proverb's honey is sweet but gathered among thorns, so the pleasure of town life is not denied, only priced.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who eat the honey of the thorny mulli plant

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the proud town-dweller who has not reckoned how long wealth and life will last

pazhamozhi.applied_to: pleasures taken without counting their end are sweetness bought with wounds

394.reading: The speaker tells his heart that it goes after the hard-hearted, longing for their way, and has today been brought low, and bids it go and not die, as others do, pointing to the house and speaking fondly of it, for wives and children are many bonds.
394.nuance: The verse is an address to one's own heart, so the counsel is self-persuasion. வன்னெஞ்சினார் may be the hard-hearted world the heart longs after, or it may praise the renouncers as hard against attachment; the sense of the first two lines turns on this. கட்டம் may be a bond or a hardship; both suit the proverb.
394.domain_note: a man urging his own heart to leave the house

pazhamozhi.literal: wives and children are many bonds

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the heart that clings to home as death nears

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attachment to wife and children holds the heart back from release

395.reading: The verse asks the lord of the hill country, where the roaring cascade falls on the millet field, what further tie is left for those who have renounced after giving up even their dear children and the wealth they earned, and says that clinging still would be like the elephant passing through while its tail does not.
395.nuance: The proverb inverts the scale: the elephant (children and wealth) has gone through the gap, and it is the tail, the smallest remnant of attachment, that sticks. The verse thus says the hardest part of renunciation is not the great surrender but the trifle kept after it.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way the elephant goes through but its tail does not

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a renouncer who keeps some small tie after leaving children and wealth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small attachment kept after a great renunciation defeats it

396.reading: Though people fear that the fruit of deeds gathered over many births will come home to the body, the verse says we see them unable to do anything at all at the place where it must be discharged, and closes with a proverb about what a pit cannot do for a pit.
396.nuance: கழிப்புழி, 'where it is to be worked off', seems to be the present life in which the deed's fruit falls due. The proverb குழிப்புழி ஆற்றா குழிக்கு is hard to construe; it may say that what fills one hole cannot fill another, or that a pit cannot be filled from within itself. The application is therefore uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: at the pit's place, they are of no avail for the pit (sense unclear)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who fear karmic fruit yet do nothing when it must be worked off

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fear of deeds' fruit is useless without acting when the fruit comes due

397.reading: A flame burns with the wick, the lamp-bowl and the ghee as its supports, and when one looks closely, so the self that runs free of its supports cuts off birth; the proverb says that when the water is gone, what depends on water is gone too.
397.nuance: The lamp is an image of dependence: the flame is real but lives only on what holds it, so release is put as the end of supports, not the destruction of the self. The verse names no subject for ஓடிப் பிறப்பறுக்கும்; the self or the knower is supplied. சுடரே ரனைத்தாய் is oddly divided in the text.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the water dries up, what relies on water dries up too

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to birth, which ceases when its supports are removed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: cutting the supports of attachment ends rebirth

398.reading: Knowing that the people of the sea-girdled world are lovers of whatever path they follow, the verse tells the lord of the forest country that people practise nothing else, and closes with the proverb that what is practised becomes heaven.
398.nuance: The first lines are hard to construe: அந்நெறி காதலர் may mean that people love the path they are used to, so that habit rules them, or that they love 'that path' of release. The proverb then says either that habit makes its own heaven or that steady practice of the good wins heaven.

pazhamozhi.literal: what one has practised becomes heaven

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to people's attachment to the path they follow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: practice persisted in becomes the next world one reaches

399.reading: The verse says not to run along the many paths of the widespread doctrines but to think on, understand and take up the complete vision, which gives greatness without limit, and closes with a proverb that the paramburi always comes to a pathakku.
399.nuance: நிரம்பிய காட்சி, 'the full seeing', in a Jain text may name right faith or right vision, the first of the three jewels, against the doctrines of other schools. பரம்பூரி and பதக்கு (a grain measure) make an obscure proverb: it may say that whatever is filled heaped comes in the end to one fixed measure, so that the many ways yield one result, but this is a guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: the paramburi always comes to a pathakku (sense unclear)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who run after many doctrines instead of one complete vision

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one complete vision is worth more than many scattered creeds

links.note: Kural 122 says to guard restraint as wealth, since life has no greater gain; Pazhamozhi 387 sets self-possession above uncounted wealth, good birth, royal property and a king's praise, for both worlds.
links.teaches: The couplet's metaphor of restraint as wealth becomes a contest here: self-mastery is weighed against real wealth, lineage and court honour and wins in this life and the next, so the figure is cashed out as a ranking.
links.list_adds: it names the rivals that restraint outranks, wealth, birth, royal goods and royal recognition, and extends the claim over both lives.

links.note: Kural 126 says drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a safeguard (ஏமம்) for seven; Pazhamozhi 388 mocks those who do not guard the five early and so make no safeguard (ஏமம்) for the road after the body.
links.teaches: Both use the same pair, guarding the five and the safeguard it earns, but the Pazhamozhi adds a deadline: the couplet promises a return across births, the proverb shows the loss of one who begins only when the body is falling.
links.list_adds: it joins the guarding of the five to the 'three' taken up, puts the act in youth (சிறுகாலை), and turns the couplet's promise into a jibe at the late starter.

links.note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by going the outer way if household life is lived in virtue; Pazhamozhi 389 asks what use is a body that does not renounce once friends, peace, marriage and the house are achieved.
links.teaches: The two rhetorical questions face each other: on the reading that the Kural's 'outer way' is renunciation, it makes a virtuous household sufficient, while the Pazhamozhi makes the finished household only the stage before the renunciation that alone gives the body its use.
links.list_adds: it lists the household's tasks (friends made, enemies quieted, a wife joined, a house set up) as completed, so household life becomes a sequence that ends, not a sufficient path.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 389 says the body that does not renounce after the household is useless; 390 says those who choose neither household nor renunciation lose both.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses give an order and a warning: household life first, renunciation after, and the one fault both condemn is the man who stops in between, holding neither.

links.note: Naladiyar 365 ranks striving in austerity first and dwelling with loved ones as the middle way; Pazhamozhi 390 condemns those who stand in the middle, choosing neither household nor its absence.
links.teaches: The word 'middle' moves: for the Naladiyar the middle is the household, a lesser but honest life, while for the Pazhamozhi the middle is indecision between the two lives, and only that is worthless, so neither life is shamed, only failing to commit.
links.list_adds: it drops the ranking of the two lives and puts the fault in the gap between them, with the image of a pole-carrier who drops both loads.

links.note: Naladiyar 6 says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped (கூற்றம் குதித்துய்ந்தார் ஈங்கில்லை) and urges the wealthy to give; Pazhamozhi 391 closes on the same words as a proverb after a list of wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and birth.
links.teaches: The same saying about leaping Death serves two ends: the Naladiyar draws from it a duty to give wealth now, the Pazhamozhi uses it to cancel every advantage of fortune and birth at once, showing the saying was a common proof for different counsels.
links.list_adds: it sets six goods (wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth, birth) before the saying, so the proverb strikes a whole inventory, where the Naladiyar names wealth alone.

links.note: Naladiyar 53 lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as impermanent and says the best renounce them; Pazhamozhi 391 lists wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and birth and says they give no escape from Death.
links.teaches: Two nearly identical lists of six goods lead to different conclusions: the Naladiyar argues from their passing to renunciation, the Pazhamozhi only to their powerlessness before Death, leaving the remedy to the verses around it.
links.list_adds: it adds birth (இற்பிறப்பு) and lustre to the goods that fail and drops home and repute, so lineage too is placed among the things Death ignores.

links.note: Naladiyar 130 asks the heart how long it thinks it will live while it clings to home and pines for children; Pazhamozhi 394 bids the heart not to die speaking fondly of the house, since wives and children are many bonds.
links.teaches: Both speakers argue with their own heart about house and children, and together they show the form: the Naladiyar shows the heart its brief span and the good deeds that alone remain, the Pazhamozhi pictures the deathbed scene of one still talking of home.
links.list_adds: it names wives and children together as many bonds in a proverb, and sets the scene at death, where the quatrain asks a question about years.

links.note: Kural 345 asks what further tie (தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்) is left to those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; Pazhamozhi 395 asks the same question (தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்) of those who left children and wealth, and answers with the elephant whose tail sticks.
links.teaches: The Pazhamozhi repeats the Kural's very question, and its proverb supplies what the couplet's 'even the body is excess' leaves unpictured: the danger after renunciation is not the great ties but a small remnant that holds the whole back.
links.list_adds: it names what was given up, dear children and earned wealth, and adds the image of the stuck tail, which ranks the last small tie as the real obstacle.

links.note: Kural 359 says one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish is freed from clinging pains; Pazhamozhi 397 shows a flame living on wick, bowl and ghee and says that, its supports gone, the self cuts off birth.
links.teaches: The Kural's abstract play on சார்பு gets a working model in the lamp: the flame is not destroyed by being blown out but goes out when what feeds it is gone, so release is shown as starvation of support, not an act of force.
links.list_adds: it lists the flame's three supports, wick, bowl and ghee, and adds the water proverb, so the couplet's one word becomes a concrete chain of dependence.

source_issues: All verses of this chapter (387-399) are flagged site_diff: the comparison site lacks them, so the text could not be checked against a second witness.
398 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at பயின்றது but has no closing mark; the proverb is taken to run to the end of the verse.
392 line 3: திச்சென்று is obscure and may be corrupt.
396 line 4: the proverb குழிப்புழி ஆற்றா குழிக்கு is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
397 line 2: சுடரே ரனைத்தாய் is oddly divided (perhaps சுடர் ஏர் அனைத்தாய்).
388 line 4: கொல்லி is obscure; it may stand for கொள்ளி.
